PROOF MECHANICS

Hoare triples and wp

Every protocol step in DyLean has a spec of the form HoareTriple step pre post, and almost all of them say pre = True and post = True. That looks empty and is the source of most confusion. The content is hidden in the definition of wp: a triple always promises that the global invariant is preserved, and that promise is what forces every append inside the step to be justified. This page builds that up from the definitions.

1 · The idea in one paragraph

A protocol step is a program that reads and appends to the trace. Its Hoare triple says: if you start from a trace satisfying the invariant and the precondition, then running the step produces a trace that still satisfies the invariant, extends the old one, and satisfies the postcondition. "Satisfies the invariant" means every entry was allowed when appended, so proving a step's triple means proving, for each append, that its entry invariant held at that moment. Triples for small actions compose into triples for whole steps through a bind rule, and the step tactic applies that rule one action at a time.

2 · Two traces

Programs run on the execution trace: what really happened, what the attacker sees. Proofs talk about the proof trace: the same entries, plus ghost annotations that exist only for the proof, such as the label chosen for each random value. tr.erase drops the annotations.

def Traceful (a: Type) := (trIn: ExecTrace) → Option a × { trOut: ExecTrace // trIn ≤ trOut }

A Traceful program takes an execution trace and returns an optional result and a longer trace. none means the program failed, for example a parse failed or a guard was false. The trace can only grow; that is built into the type.

3 · What wp says

WP.wp f post tr is the weakest precondition: the condition on a proof trace tr under which running f ends well, where "well" means post plus the built-in obligations. For Traceful:

instance : WP Traceful where
  wp f post tr_proof :=
    let (opt_x, tr_exec') := f.run tr_proof.erase      -- run the program on the execution view
    ∃ tr_proof',                                      -- there is a new proof trace…
      ( match opt_x with
        | .none   => True                             -- …failure: no postcondition owed
        | .some x => post x tr_proof' ) ∧             -- …success: the postcondition on the new trace
      Trace.Invariant tr_proof' ∧                     -- …that satisfies the invariant
      tr_exec' = tr_proof'.erase ∧                    -- …that erases to what the program produced
      tr_proof ≤ tr_proof'                            -- …and extends the old proof trace

Field by field

∃ tr_proof'Choosing the witness means choosing the ghost annotations for the entries the program just appended. This is where ghost arguments come from.
Trace.Invariant tr_proof'The new trace satisfies the invariant. This conjunct is in every wp, which is why a triple with trivial pre and post is not trivial.
tr_exec' = tr_proof'.eraseThe proof trace really is an annotation of what the program did, not an invented trace.
tr_proof ≤ tr_proof'The proof trace only grows, so facts stated about the old trace can be carried to the new one.
Failure is not an escape hatch. When the program fails, the postcondition is True, but the invariant, erasure and extension are still required. A step that appends two entries and then fails must have justified those two entries. Correctness of post is partial; preservation of the invariant is total.

The other two instances: Id and Err

For pure computations there is no trace to change. wp f post tr := post f.run tr for Id, and for Err, which is OptionT Id and is used by parsing, failure again owes nothing. These exist so the same triple vocabulary covers parsers and pure helpers, which are then lifted into Traceful.

4 · Hoare triples

def hoareTriple (f: m a) (pre: ProofTrace → Prop) (post: a → ProofTrace → Prop) : Prop :=
  ∀ tr, pre tr → Trace.Invariant tr → WP.wp f post tr

class HoareTriple (f: m a) (pre: outParam (ProofTrace → Prop)) (post: outParam (a → ProofTrace → Prop)) where
  pf: hoareTriple f pre post

The definition adds one assumption to wp: the starting trace satisfies the invariant. So a triple reads "invariant and pre before, invariant and post after".

The class form matters for automation. pre and post are outParams, so typeclass search on HoareTriple f ?pre ?post finds the spec of f and reports its pre and post. Specs are declared as @[instance] theorem X.spec : HoareTriple …, which is why proving a step never names the specs of the actions it calls.

Ghost arguments

Some specs need a value that does not appear in the program. genRand 32 produces fresh bytes, but which label do they get? The program has no label; the proof chooses one. A ghost triple is indexed by such a value:

class HoareTripleGhost (f: m a) [HasGhostArgumentType f g] (ghost: g) (pre: outParam …) (post: outParam …) where
  pf: hoareTriple f pre post

theorem genRand.spec (size) (label: Bytes → Label) (usage: Usage) :
  HoareTripleGhost (genRand size) (label, usage)
    (fun _ => True)
    (fun res tr => res.Invariant tr ∧ res.label tr = label res ∧ res.HasUsage usage tr)

In a proof the ghost is supplied with step with ⟨ … ⟩. Client.initiate.spec writes step with ⟨ fun xSk => clientLabel me (dhPk xSk), Usage.nothing ⟩: the label of xSk is declared to be the client's label for its own public key. Every plain triple counts as a ghost triple with ghost (). Ghost types in the library:

actionghostwhat it decides
appendEntry eNat → ProofEntryTthe proof entry recorded, as a function of the timestamp
genRand n(Bytes → Label) × Usagethe label and usage of the fresh bytes
sign sk n mUsagethe usage of the key, which the signing predicate inspects
forIn xs init fLoopInvariantAndProofa loop invariant and a triple for one iteration

When no ghost is given, step can look for one: a ghost "metaprogram" may search the context, as sign's does for a hypothesis sk.HasUsage ?u.

Pure triples

Cryptographic operations such as dhPk, dh, hash and sign are values, not trace actions. They get HoareTriplePure: no trace change, just "if pre holds on this trace, post holds of the value".

class HoareTriplePure (x: a) (pre: outParam (ProofTrace → Prop)) (post: outParam (a → ProofTrace → Prop)) where
  pf: ∀ tr, pre tr → post x tr

instance (sk: Bytes) : HoareTriplePure (dhPk sk)
  (fun tr => sk.Invariant tr)
  (fun res tr => res.Invariant tr ∧ res.label tr = Label.pub)

A guard (verify …) line uses a bridge instance that turns the pure triple of the boolean into a triple for the guard, with true substituted. That is how a passed signature check becomes a hypothesis.

5 · The base case: appending

Every action that writes to the trace bottoms out in appendEntry, whose spec is the only place an invariant is checked directly:

theorem appendEntry.spec (execEntry) (mkProofEntry: Nat → ProofEntryT) :
  HoareTripleGhost (appendEntry execEntry) (mkProofEntry)
    (fun tr => ∀ time, ErasableProofEntry.erase (mkProofEntry time) = execEntry ∧
                       SubTraceInvariant.invariant tr (mkProofEntry time))     -- the entry invariant, before
    (fun time tr => tr.at? time = some (mkProofEntry time))                    -- the entry is there, after
-- proof: the witness is the old proof trace with (mkProofEntry trProof.length) appended

The precondition is the entry invariant on the trace before. The derived specs just instantiate it: sendMessage needs msg.Publishable, logEvent needs the event invariant, storeLocalState needs the state invariant. Reading is the converse:

theorem getEntry.spec (timestamp) : HoareTriple (getEntry timestamp)
  (fun _ => True)
  (fun entry tr => ∃ proofEntry, entry = erase proofEntry ∧
                   SubTraceInvariant.invariant (tr.prefix timestamp) proofEntry)

Reading an entry gives back the invariant that held when it was written, on the prefix up to it. That is the same fact EventLoggedAt_imp_EventInv recovers in security proofs.

6 · Chaining: the bind rule

There is no bind instance. A step's spec is proved by applying a theorem for x >>= f, once per action:

theorem Traceful.bind_wp (ghost: g) (x: Traceful a) (f: a → Traceful b) …
    [HoareTripleGhost x ghost pre_x post_x]
    (pf_tr_inv: Trace.Invariant tr)
    (pf_pre_x: pre_x tr)                                            -- prove x's precondition now
    (pf_next: ∀ tr_mid x', post_x x' tr_mid →                        -- then, for whatever x returned
                Trace.Invariant tr_mid → tr ≤ tr_mid →             --   on the longer, still-invariant trace
                WP.wp (f x') post_f tr_mid)                         --   the rest of the program is fine
  : WP.wp (x >>= f) post_f tr

Read it as a recipe: discharge x's precondition on the current trace, then continue with a fresh trace tr_mid, the result x', x's postcondition about them, the invariant, and the fact that tr_mid extends tr. finish_wp handles the last action, where the continuation is the final postcondition.

programprepost
pure xTrueres = x
failureTrueTrue
guard bTrueb
guard (v = true) with a pure triple for vv's prev's post at true
liftM x for x : Err ax's prex's post

7 · The step tactic

step automates the recipe. On a goal wp (x >>= f) post tr it:

  1. applies bind_wp, which fixes x and f by unification;
  2. takes the ghost from with ⟨ … ⟩, checking its type against the action's declared ghost type, or searches for one, or uses ();
  3. finds x's spec by typeclass search on HoareTripleGhost x ghost ?pre ?post;
  4. proves the precondition with grind, or with your tactic if you wrote step by tac;
  5. introduces the new trace, the result named after the binder in your code, and the postcondition split into separate hypotheses;
  6. moves every earlier hypothesis about the old trace to the new trace using the monotonicity lemmas, then renames the new trace back to tr, so you always see one trace.

On a let x := v it uses v's pure triple instead, and the trace does not change. A few companions handle awkward code:

tacticwhat it is for
step by tacthe precondition needs more than plain grind, typically unfolding a state invariant
step with ⟨ g ⟩supply a ghost argument
step_let x with ⟨ g ⟩prove a pure triple for a let introduced earlier
step_introintroduce a let without proving anything yet, to prove facts about it later. Server.receive does this for sig, because the event the signing predicate refers to is logged after the let
hoistpull complex arguments of the next action into separate lets, so each can be handled on its own
mark_non_monotone htell the monotonicity pass to drop h rather than transport it. logEvent.spec uses it, since an event invariant has no general "later" lemma

8 · Client.initiate, step by step

The spec is HoareTriple (Client.initiate me) (fun _ => True) (fun _ _ => True). Step through it: the left side is the program with the current action highlighted, the right side is the proof context after the tactic. Hypothesis names are as the tactic introduces them; Lean may display some as inaccessible.

The visible postconditions are all True. The real content is the hidden invariant conjunct, which forced the obligations at the event, the store and the send. The trace page shows the entries this step produces in a real run: indices 4 to 7.

9 · Monotonicity: why every fact must survive growth

After each action the trace is longer, and every earlier hypothesis was stated about the shorter trace. step transports them: for each hypothesis that mentions the old trace it asserts the same statement on the new trace and proves it with grind restricted to the grind_later lemma set. A hypothesis that cannot be transported is an error, "cannot monotonize", unless marked non-monotone.

The grind_later set contains the "later" facts the framework and protocols provide: invariants, labels, usages and publishability of bytes are stable; events stay logged; entries stay at their index; state invariants carry an invariant_later field; labels' corruption predicates must be monotone by construction. This is the same requirement that appears everywhere else in DyLean: anything stated about a trace must remain true as the trace grows, because some later proof will read it back.

10 · Where triples end up

A step's triple with pre = True and post = True is exactly what ReachableImpliesInvariant asks for. One instance per step, combined over the reachability config, and a four-line induction turns them into "every reachable trace has an invariant proof trace behind it". Security theorems apply that once and never mention a triple again.

class ReachableImpliesInvariant (config: ReachabilityConfig) where
  pf: ∀ input, HoareTriple (config.step input).snd (fun tr => config.PreCond input tr.erase) (fun _ _ => True)
The prose and the stepper are editorial, written from the source; the cards are the compiler's view of ../dylean.
